summary: This proposed standard defines MIB objects for managing the security protocols on interfaces that use the Point-to-Point Protocol family.

plainLanguage.summary: PPP connects two computers over a line, and sometimes needs a password check. This paper lists what a network manager can look up about those checks.

questions: what is the ppp security mib
how does snmp manage ppp authentication
why is the ppp security group optional
is it safe to read ppp secrets over snmp
subtitle: SNMP objects for configuring PPP authentication, including the stored identities and secrets, and why they must be locked down.

tldr.problem: A network manager who runs PPP links needs a standard way to choose which authentication protocols a link tries and to set the identities and secrets they use.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines an optional PPP Security Group of SNMP objects: one table ranks the security protocols per link, and another holds ID and secret pairs for PAP and CHAP.
tldr.outcome: Because these objects expose passwords and can switch security off, the RFC says access should only be allowed through SNMPv2 for parties that use privacy. It is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 1472 is a Proposed Standard from June 1993, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines the PPP Security Group objects, which are optional to implement.

sections.title: Where This MIB Fits
sections.content:
RFC 1472 defines a piece of the Management Information Base (MIB) for managing the security protocols on interfaces that use the family of Point-to-Point Protocols. It sits inside the Internet-standard Network Management Framework, which has three parts: the SMI (RFC 1155 and RFC 1212) for describing objects, MIB-II (RFC 1213) as the core set of objects, and SNMP (RFC 1157) as the protocol used to reach them.

Objects are written in the subset of ASN.1 that the SMI allows. Each object type is named by an OBJECT IDENTIFIER, and the object type together with an instance identifies one specific value.
sections.plainLanguage: Network managers use one shared way to describe and fetch settings from devices. This paper adds the settings for PPP password checks to that shared list.

sections.title: How PPP Is Divided Up
sections.content:
The RFC points out that PPP is not one protocol but a large family, and splits it into three rough categories.

  • Control Protocols run the PPP itself: the Link Control Protocol (LCP), the Password Authentication Protocol (PAP), the Link Quality Report (LQR) and the Challenge Handshake Authentication Protocol (CHAP).
  • Network Protocols carry the traffic. Each one encapsulates the datagrams of a higher-layer protocol, and the term does not imply an OSI Layer-3 protocol; there is, for example, a Bridging network protocol.
  • Network Control Protocols (NCPs) control the Network Protocols, generally one NCP per Network Protocol, such as the IP Control Protocol.

This document manages only one slice of that family, the PPP authentication protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: PPP is like a big toolbox with several kinds of tools. This paper only covers the tools that check who you are.

sections.title: Keeping the MIB Small
sections.content:
The authors tried to keep the MIB as simple as possible, in line with IAB directives and good engineering practice. An object was only proposed for inclusion if it passed these criteria.

  • It must be essential for fault or configuration management. Objects whose only purpose was debugging implementations were explicitly excluded.
  • There should be evidence of current use or usefulness.
  • The total number of objects is limited.
  • Objects that can simply be derived from others in this or other MIBs are left out.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors only packed what a manager really needs, like packing a small bag for a trip instead of the whole closet.

sections.title: The Security Configuration Table
sections.content:
The module PPP-SEC-MIB hangs everything under pppSecurity, which is { ppp 2 }. It first names the protocols: pppSecurityPapProtocol and pppSecurityChapMD5Protocol are object identifiers under pppSecurityProtocols.

The pppSecurityConfigTable lets the manager say which security protocols a link uses and in what order. Each row is indexed by pppSecurityConfigLink and pppSecurityConfigPreference, and also carries pppSecurityConfigProtocol and pppSecurityConfigStatus.

  • The link is an ifIndex value. A value of 0 means the default entry, which applies to every link without explicit entries.
  • Protocols with lower preference values are tried before those with higher values.
  • Setting the status to invalid(1) invalidates the row. Whether the agent removes it is implementation-specific, so management stations must be ready to see rows that are no longer in use.
sections.plainLanguage: The first table is a ranked list for each line: try this password method first, then that one if the first fails.

sections.title: The Identity and Secret Table
sections.content:
The pppSecuritySecretsTable holds the identities and secrets that the PPP authentication protocols use. It contains both the pairs the local entity will present to the remote one and the pairs it expects from the remote one. Several pairs can exist for one link, and how the local entity picks one is a local implementation decision.

Each row is indexed by pppSecuritySecretsLink and pppSecuritySecretsIdIndex. The main columns are:

  • pppSecuritySecretsDirection: local-to-remote(1) or remote-to-local(2).
  • pppSecuritySecretsProtocol: which protocol, such as PAP or CHAP, the pair applies to.
  • pppSecuritySecretsIdentity and pppSecuritySecretsSecret: octet strings of 0 to 255 bytes. For PAP they hold a Peer-ID and a password; for CHAP-MD5 they hold the CHAP NAME and the MD5 secret.

The table description expects access to be limited to SNMP party pairs for which a privacy protocol is in use for all messages.
sections.plainLanguage: The second table is a notebook of names and secret passwords, one for what I say to you and one for what you say to me.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC admits that letting an operator configure PPP authentication is itself a security risk. This MIB holds peer identities (like user IDs) and the secrets that authenticate them (like passwords), and an intruder could disable PPP security if the control variables were not protected. It lists these mitigations:

  • Risky variables are in separate, optional MIB groups, so an implementor may skip them.
  • Making them read-only is possible but not recommended, because the authentication variables can still be easily read.
  • With SNMPv2, the variables can go into MIB views reachable only by parties that use authentication and privacy, or be made inaccessible to every party. Separate tables make the right subtree easy to identify.

An implementation should allow access to this MIB only through SNMPv2 and only for privacy-enhanced parties. SNMPv1, or SNMPv2 without privacy, is called very dangerous.
sections.plainLanguage: Since the notebook holds secret passwords, only people with a special locked key should be allowed to look at it, and anyone else must be kept out.

sections.title: Groups and Conformance
sections.content:
MIB objects are arranged in groups, and a group is the basic unit of conformance: if its semantics apply to an implementation, all objects in the group must be implemented. The PPP MIB family includes the Link, LQR, LQR Extensions, IP, Bridge and Security groups, and this document specifies only the PPP Security Group.

Implementing the Security Group is optional. Because it controls security functions, its variables should be protected by SNMPv2 security, and an agent that does not support SNMPv2 with privacy is strongly advised not to implement the group.
sections.plainLanguage: Devices may skip this chapter. If a device cannot keep secrets safe on the way, it is better that it leaves the chapter out.
